claims.text: Pressure-assisted copper infiltration followed by hot-isostatic pressing will produce a near-fully dense W–Cu composite.
The proposed process will significantly reduce porosity relative to conventional infiltration-based routes.
Reduced porosity will enhance mechanical durability and thermal conductivity.
The starting material is a partially sintered, connected W preform with intentionally retained porosity for Cu infiltration.
Copper infiltration is to be conducted at approximately 1100–1200 °C and approximately 10^-4 Torr.
The infiltration is to be followed by HIP at approximately 100 MPa and 1200 °C for about one hour.
A high-vacuum environment will minimize Cu oxidation and vaporization.
Sub-boiling-temperature infiltration will minimize Cu volatilization and oxidation.
HIP will collapse residual pores and densify the W–Cu microstructure.
Collapsing residual pores will improve W–Cu interfacial bonding and mechanical integrity.
The resulting composite will exceed 98% relative density.
The resulting composite will have greater fracture toughness and mechanical strength than a conventionally infiltrated W–Cu composite.
The resulting composite will have higher thermal conductivity than a conventionally infiltrated W–Cu composite.
The resulting W–Cu composite will be suitable for long-term heat extraction in irradiated fusion-reactor joints.
Conventional Cu infiltration into W skeletons at higher temperature or ambient pressure often produces excessive porosity, incomplete bonding, and suboptimal mechanical properties.
Operation above approximately 1200 °C or at insufficient vacuum will cause substantial Cu vaporization and oxidation.
Extremely large parts may require process modifications.
The proposed material's performance and microstructural stability under sustained, intense neutron flux over reactor timescales remain unverified.
Fusion-facing components must tolerate high temperatures, high heat loads, and intense particle and neutron irradiation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies approximately 10^-4 Torr as a sufficient high vacuum but says that pressure below 10^-4 Torr represents insufficient vacuum. Lower absolute pressure corresponds to a stronger vacuum, so the stated boundary direction is internally reversed.
